title: Cig kofte
subtitle: Bulgur and tomato paste rolls with walnuts and herbs
excerpt: Cig kofte (literally raw kofte) are hand-kneaded patties of fine bulgur, tomato paste, walnuts, and fresh herbs. Despite the name, the modern version is entirely grain-based with no raw meat: the bulgur softens through kneading alone. They are eaten cold or at room temperature, wrapped in lettuce or flatbread.
sourceNotes: Aylin Oney Tan, A Taste of Sun and Fire: Gaziantep Cookery (2014). Cig kofte documented as a southeastern Turkish street food originating in Urfa. Paula Wolfert, The Cooking of the Eastern Mediterranean (1994). Notes on the grain-based modern version and regional variations.

recipe.batchNotes: Doubles easily. Keeps in the fridge for two days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to two days ahead and refrigerate. Bring to room temperature before serving.

content.text: Cig kofte are cold, hand-formed patties of fine bulgur wheat worked with tomato paste, walnuts, and herbs until the grain softens through kneading alone. No cooking is involved. The name means 'raw kofte' and refers to an older version made with raw meat; the modern grain-only version is widely sold as street food across Turkey. The patties are eaten wrapped in lettuce leaves or flatbread with a squeeze of lemon and pomegranate molasses.

items.prepNote: as a substitute for pomegranate molasses

content.text: Use the finest-grind bulgur available, sold as number 1 or 'extra fine'. Coarser grinds will not soften sufficiently without cooking. Lettuce leaves or flatbread to wrap and serve.
Put {{bulgur-wheat}} into a large bowl. Pour over 250 ml of cold water and stir once. Leave for five minutes until the water is absorbed and the bulgur has swollen slightly.

Add {{tomato-puree}}, {{sea-salt-fine}}, {{aleppo-pepper}}, {{cumin-ground}}, and {{black-pepper}}. Begin kneading the mixture with your hands, working it firmly for ten minutes. The heat of your hands and the pressure help the bulgur soften. The mixture should become cohesive and slightly tacky.
Add {{walnuts}}, {{spring-onion}}, {{parsley-flat}}, and {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}}. Knead for five more minutes until the mix is even and holds its shape when pressed.
Cover and rest at room temperature for 30 minutes. Shape into small oval patties (or squeeze into any shape) with wet hands. Serve with lemon juice and date syrup if using.

items.symptom: The bulgur is still gritty after kneading
items.cause: Bulgur grind too coarse or not kneaded long enough
items.fix: Only extra-fine (number 1) bulgur works raw. Coarser versions need cooking. Knead for at least fifteen minutes in total.

items.symptom: The mixture won't hold a shape
items.cause: Too much water or not enough kneading
items.fix: Keep kneading: the mixture tightens as the starch is worked. If it is still very loose, add another tablespoon of bulgur.

items.cause: The seasoning needs to be quite bold to come through
items.fix: Taste the mixture before resting and add more salt and aleppo pepper if needed. The flavour should be punchy.

items.symptom: The patties dry out quickly after shaping
items.fix: Cover with cling film or a damp cloth. Cig kofte dries quickly if left exposed to air.

content.text: Cig kofte originated in southeastern Turkey, particularly in Sanliurfa (Urfa), where the original version was made by kneading raw minced lamb with fine bulgur until the grain absorbed the meat juices. As raw meat became a health concern and was eventually banned in commercial food, the grain-only version emerged and became its own distinct dish. It is now one of the most common Turkish street foods, sold from carts, franchised chains, and market stalls across the country. The vendor adds pomegranate molasses and a squeeze of lemon; the customer wraps it in a fresh romaine leaf. The dish is also made at home in southeastern Turkey as part of a meze spread.
